vignette:
She is a 22-year-old Latin American woman who comes into treatment carrying an exhaustion that seems older than her years. She works as an accountant, a job that suits the parts of her that like order, numbers, and predictable systems, but lately even spreadsheets and deadlines feel harder to hold onto. Before the illness, her life is small but steady: work during the week, calls with her mother, occasional dinners with cousins, and a quiet sense that the future is something she can plan for in columns and categories. She is single, and at first that has felt manageable, even preferable, because her attention is divided between work, family, and the ordinary ambitions of being a young adult.

Everything changes when her child becomes critically ill. The illness comes quickly, with the kind of urgency that does not allow her to build up to it emotionally. One day she is moving through her routine, and the next she is in hospitals, answering questions she does not understand, signing forms with a hand that will not stay still, and watching doctors use words like “serious” and “uncertain” while she tries to make sense of what they are saying. She remembers the first time she sees her child hooked up to machines and feels her own body go cold, as if something inside her has stepped away to survive the moment. In those days, she stops thinking in terms of morning and night; everything becomes a sequence of alarms, waiting rooms, updates, and fear.

At the hospital, she learns to read tiny changes in her child’s breathing and expression, and she becomes hyper-alert in a way that never fully turns off. Even after the immediate crisis passes, her mind keeps returning to the worst possibilities. She replayes conversations with doctors, searching for signs she missed, wondering if she should have insisted on care sooner, done more, noticed more. Guilt settles into her like a second skin. She tells herself repeatedly that her child is alive now, that the worst has passed, but her nervous system does not seem to believe her. She startles at sudden noises, especially alarms, and she cannot sit through medical dramas or even certain commercials without feeling her chest tighten.

Returning to work is one of the first places her distress becomes visible in daily life. As an accountant, she is expected to be precise, calm, and focused, but she finds that numbers blur when she is tired, and she has to reread the same line several times before it makes sense. She keeps her phone close on her desk and checks it obsessively, unable to tolerate even a few minutes without knowing whether there is an update from home. When a coworker mentions a child’s fever or a hospital bill, she feels a sharp wave of nausea and has to step away. She begins arriving early so she can catch up before others are around, and she works harder than before, as if perfect performance might compensate for the helplessness she felt when her child was sick. Still, there are days when she stares at a ledger and realizes she has not absorbed a single page.

At home, sleep does not bring real rest. She falls asleep only after prolonged effort and wakes often, sometimes with the impression that she has heard a monitor beeping or a nurse calling her name. Some nights she lies awake listening for her child’s breathing even when the child is doing well, a habit that leaves her tense and irritable by morning. She has become more guarded with other people. Friends ask how she is doing, and she answers with a practiced “fine,” because the full story feels too large and too frightening to place in conversation. She avoids talking about the hospitalization unless she has to, yet she also cannot stop thinking about it. Certain smells, hospital corridors, and even the sight of a white coat can bring the memories back with a force that feels immediate rather than remembered.

Although she is young, she speaks about the experience with a heaviness that suggests she has been carrying it for a long time. She loves her child deeply and is grateful for survival, but gratitude does not erase what happened. Part of her remains in the hospital room, watching the monitors, bracing for bad news, trying to stay composed while everything inside her is breaking apart. In sessions, she often pauses as if checking whether she is allowed to say how afraid she was, and when she does, her voice softens. She is not the person she was before the illness, and she knows it. She is still learning how to live in the present while her body continues to behave as though danger could return at any moment.
